( = <reference osisRef="Matt.13.54-Matt.13.58">Mt 13:54-58</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:16-30</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26889" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.30">Lu 4:16-30</reference>.<div eID="gen26889" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.6.7-Mark.6.13">Mr 6:7-13</reference>. Mission of the Twelve Apostles. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.10.1">Mt 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">5-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.1-Luke.9.6">Lu 9:1-6</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26890" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.1">Mt 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">Mt 10:5-15</reference>.<div eID="gen26890" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.6.14-Mark.6.29">Mr 6:14-29</reference>. Herod Thinks Jesus a Resurrection of the Murdered Baptist--Account of His Death. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12">Mt 14:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.7-Luke.9.9">Lu 9:7-9</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26891" type="x-p"/> Herod's View of Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.14-Mark.6.16">Mr 6:14-16</reference>).<div eID="gen26891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13964"/><hi type="bold">14. And King Herod--</hi>that is, Herod Antipas, one of the three sons of Herod the Great, and own brother of Archelaus (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.22">Mt 2:22</reference>), who ruled as ethnarch over Galilee and Perea.<div eID="gen26892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard of him; (for his name was spread abroad); and he said--</hi>"unto his servants" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.2">Mt 14:2</reference>), his councillors or court ministers.<div eID="gen26893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That John the Baptist was risen from the dead--</hi>The murdered prophet haunted his guilty breast like a specter, and seemed to him alive again and clothed with unearthly powers, in the person of Jesus. <div eID="gen26894" type="x-p"/>
entries.2bf5650223001bd46a554d19f4d96e05c46ebc1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13965"/><div sID="gen26895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13965"/><hi type="bold">15. Others said, That it is Elias. And others, That it is a prophet, or as one of the prophets--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.16.14">Mt 16:14</reference>). <div eID="gen26895" type="x-p"/>
entries.0be74c2ddb824b5ad0a0e681441f6d9ca1a4299b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13966"/><div sID="gen26896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13966"/><hi type="bold">16. But when Herod heard thereof, he said, It is John, whom I beheaded; he is risen from the dead--</hi>"Himself has risen"; as if the innocence and sanctity of his faithful reprover had not suffered that he should lie long dead.<div eID="gen26896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26897" type="x-p"/> Account of the Baptist's Imprisonment and Death (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.17-Mark.6.29">Mr 6:17-29</reference>). <div eID="gen26897" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e94a3be716c0f8160b8ae9120f9edb25e8f97c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13967"/><div sID="gen26898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13967"/><hi type="bold">17. For Herod himself had sent forth, and laid hold upon John, and bound him in prison--</hi>in the castle of Machærus, near the southern extremity of Herod's dominions, and adjoining the Dead Sea [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.5,2].<div eID="gen26898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for Herodias' sake--</hi>She was the granddaughter of Herod the Great.<div eID="gen26899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his brother Philip's wife--</hi>and therefore the niece of both brothers. This Philip, however, was not the tetrarch of that name mentioned in <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1">Lu 3:1</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1">Lu 3:1</reference>), but one whose distinctive name was "Herod Philip," another son of Herod the Great--who was disinherited by his father. Herod Antipas' own wife was the daughter of Aretas, king of Arabia; but he prevailed on Herodias, his half-brother Philip's wife, to forsake her husband and live with him, on condition, says Josephus [Antiquities, 18.5,1], that he should put away his own wife. This involved him afterwards in war with Aretas, who totally defeated him and destroyed his army, from the effects of which he was never able to recover himself. <div eID="gen26900" type="x-p"/>
entries.4324ad4453dcd4d16f9903848332dd4b2c580a51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13968"/><div sID="gen26901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13968"/><hi type="bold">18. For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife--</hi>Noble fidelity! It was not lawful because Herod's wife and Herodias' husband were both living; and further, because the parties were within the forbidden degrees of consanguinity (see <reference osisRef="Lev.20.21">Le 20:21</reference>); Herodias being the daughter of Aristobulus, the brother of both Herod and Philip [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.5,4]. <div eID="gen26901" type="x-p"/>
entries.795185fece70e0219417fd82fdfc5c148afe731e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13969"/><div sID="gen26902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13969"/><hi type="bold">19. Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him--</hi>rather, as in the Margin, "had a grudge against him." Probably she was too proud to speak to him; still less would she quarrel with him.<div eID="gen26902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26903" type="x-p"/> and would have killed him; but she could not. <div eID="gen26903" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff87f1e4c0d29a4cea3ef878bdd72894538085e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13970"/><div sID="gen26904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13970"/><hi type="bold">20. For Herod feared John--</hi>but, as Bengel notes, John feared not Herod.<div eID="gen26904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowing that he was a just man and an holy--</hi>Compare the case of Elijah with Ahab, after the murder of Naboth (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.20">1Ki 21:20</reference>).<div eID="gen26905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and observed him--</hi>rather, as in the Margin, "kept" or "saved him"; that is, from the wicked designs of Herodias, who had been watching for some pretext to get Herod entangled and committed to despatch him.<div eID="gen26906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when he heard him, he did many things--</hi>many good things under the influence of the Baptist on his conscience.<div eID="gen26907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and heard him gladly--</hi>a striking statement this, for which we are indebted to our graphic Evangelist alone, illustrating the working of contrary principles in the slaves of passion. But this only shows how far Herodias must have wrought upon him, as Jezebel upon Ahab, that he should at length agree to what his awakened conscience kept him long from executing. <div eID="gen26908" type="x-p"/>
entries.56d21c2e170cd14ed0f2a16a5524bbe94fc9d7e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13971"/><div sID="gen26909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13971"/><hi type="bold">21. And when a convenient day--</hi>for the purposes of Herodias.<div eID="gen26909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was come, that Herod--</hi>rather, "A convenient day being come, when Herod."<div eID="gen26910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on his birthday, made a supper to his lords, high captains, and chief estates of Galilee--</hi>This graphic minuteness of detail adds much to the interest of the tragic narrative. <div eID="gen26911" type="x-p"/>
entries.51b987d1243ab90e3df1c0bb8d5cb77fa12788b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13972"/><div sID="gen26912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13972"/><hi type="bold">22. And when the daughter of the said Herodias--</hi>that is, her daughter by her proper husband, Herod Philip: Her name was Salome [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.5,4].<div eID="gen26912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came in and danced, and pleased Herod and them that sat with him, the king said unto the damsel--</hi>"the girl" (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.42">Mr 5:42</reference>).<div eID="gen26913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26914" type="x-p"/> Ask of me whatsoever thou wilt, and I will give it thee. <div eID="gen26914" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c39f57dcfb4a40638b0c900938ebd9c352eb9f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13973"/><div sID="gen26915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13973"/><hi type="bold">23. And he--</hi>the king, so called, but only by courtesy (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.14">Mr 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen26915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sware unto her Whatsoever thou shalt ask of me, unto the half of my kingdom--</hi>Those in whom passion and luxury have destroyed self-command will in a capricious moment say and do what in their cool moments they bitterly regret. <div eID="gen26916" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0bd0f39757640aa326f2d9562fa60291ff83a95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13974"/><div sID="gen26917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13974"/><hi type="bold">24. And she said, The head of John the Baptist--</hi>Abandoned women are more shameless and heartless than men. The Baptist's fidelity marred the pleasures of Herodias, and this was too good an opportunity of getting rid of him to let slip. <div eID="gen26917" type="x-p"/>
entries.87dbcfcc4d72ee598425eb8550775e1cb4045818: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13975"/><div sID="gen26918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13975"/><hi type="bold">25. I will that thou give me by and by--</hi>rather, "at once."<div eID="gen26918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a charger--</hi>large, flat trencher.<div eID="gen26919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26920" type="x-p"/> the head of John the Baptist. <div eID="gen26920" type="x-p"/>
entries.72771d14df5a759cebea0080e1c67a08171bbf8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13976"/><div sID="gen26921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13976"/><hi type="bold">26. And the king was exceeding sorry--</hi>With his feelings regarding John, and the truths which so told upon his conscience from that preacher's lips, and after so often and carefully saving him from his paramour's rage, it must have been very galling to find himself at length entrapped by his own rash folly.<div eID="gen26921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet for his oath's sake--</hi>See how men of no principle, but troublesome conscience, will stick at breaking a rash oath, while yielding to the commission of the worst crimes!<div eID="gen26922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and for their sakes which sat with him--</hi>under the influence of that false shame, which could not brook being thought to be troubled with religious or moral scruples. To how many has this proved a fatal snare!<div eID="gen26923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26924" type="x-p"/> he would not reject her. <div eID="gen26924" type="x-p"/>
entries.d50d5bc21d8e6f7c24c519d78ad63aab2e1f4a0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13977"/><div sID="gen26925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13977"/><hi type="bold">27. And immediately the king sent an executioner--</hi>one of the guards in attendance. The word is Roman, denoting one of the Imperial Guard.<div eID="gen26925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison--</hi>after, it would seem, more than twelve months' imprisonment. Blessed martyr! Dark and cheerless was the end reserved for thee: but now thou hast thy Master's benediction, "Blessed is he whosoever shall not be offended in Me" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.6">Mt 11:6</reference>), and hast found the life thou gavest away (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.39">Mt 10:39</reference>). But where are they in whose skirts is found thy blood? <div eID="gen26926" type="x-p"/>
entries.6679f04ee04d4deaa48e7bac9466503a9fe2c9f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13978"/><div sID="gen26927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13978"/><hi type="bold">28. And brought his head in a charger, and gave it to the damsel: and the damsel gave it to her mother--</hi>Herodias did not shed the blood of the stern reprover; she only got it done, and then gloated over it, as it streamed from the trunkless head. <div eID="gen26927" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5619afd03b08876338c39298632ed8434c35037: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13979"/><div sID="gen26928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13979"/><hi type="bold">29. And when his disciples heard of it--</hi>that is, the Baptist's own disciples.<div eID="gen26928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they came and took up his corpse, and laid it in a tomb--</hi>"and went and told Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.12">Mt 14:12</reference>). If these disciples had, up to this time, stood apart from Him, as adherents of John (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.2">Mt 11:2</reference>), perhaps they now came to Jesus, not without some secret reflection on Him for His seeming neglect of their master; but perhaps, too, as orphans, to cast in their lot henceforth with the Lord's disciples. How Jesus felt, or what He said, on receiving this intelligence, is not recorded; but He of whom it was said, as He stood by the grave of His friend Lazarus, "Jesus wept," was not likely to receive such intelligence without deep emotion. And one reason why He might not be unwilling that a small body of John's disciples should cling to him to the last, might be to provide some attached friends who should do for his precious body, on a small scale, what was afterwards to be done for His own.<div eID="gen26929" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.6.30-Mark.6.56">Mr 6:30-56</reference>. The Twelve on Their Return, Having Reported the Success of Their Mission, Jesus Crosses the Sea of Galilee with Them, Teaches the People, and Miraculously Feeds Them to the Number of Five Thousand--He Sends His Disciples by Ship Again to the Western Side, While He Himself Returns Afterwards Walking on the Sea--Incidents on Landing. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.14.13-Matt.14.36">Mt 14:13-36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.10-Luke.9.17">Lu 9:10-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.1-John.6.24">Joh 6:1-24</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> Here, for the first time, all the four streams of sacred text run parallel. The occasion and all the circumstances of this grand section are thus brought before us with a vividness quite remarkable.<div eID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> Five Thousand Miraculously Fed (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.30-Mark.6.44">Mr 6:30-44</reference>). <div eID="gen26931" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d7775b23a16ca1cbc212c242b7ea2a04157674f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13980"/><div sID="gen26932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13980"/><hi type="bold">30. And the apostles gathered themselves together--</hi>probably at Capernaum, on returning from their mission (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.7-Mark.6.13">Mr 6:7-13</reference>).<div eID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and told him all things, both what they had done, and what they had taught--</hi>Observe the various reasons He had for crossing to the other side. First, Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.13">Mt 14:13</reference>) says, that "when Jesus heard" of the murder of His faithful forerunner--from those attached disciples of his who had taken up his body and laid it in a sepulchre (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.29">Mr 6:29</reference>)--"He departed by ship into a desert place apart"; either to avoid some apprehended consequences to Himself, arising from the Baptist's death (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.23">Mt 10:23</reference>), or more probably to be able to indulge in those feelings which that affecting event had doubtless awakened, and to which the bustle of the multitude around Him was very unfavorable. Next, since He must have heard the report of the Twelve with the deepest interest, and probably with something of the emotion which He experienced on the return of the Seventy (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.10.17-Luke.10.22">Lu 10:17-22</reference>), He sought privacy for undisturbed reflection on this begun preaching and progress of His kingdom. Once more, He was wearied with the multitude of "comers and goers"--depriving Him even of leisure enough to take His food--and wanted rest: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while," &c. Under the combined influence of all these considerations, our Lord sought this change. <div eID="gen26933" type="x-p"/>
entries.785679dc1b74db5efacbe9c1c35af2aca5d7d623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13981"/><div sID="gen26934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13981"/><hi type="bold">32. And they departed into a desert place by ship privately--</hi>"over the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias," says John (<reference osisRef="John.6.1">Joh 6:1</reference>), the only one of the Evangelists who so fully describes it; the others having written when their readers were supposed to know something of it, while the last wrote for those at a greater distance of time and place. This "desert place" is more definitely described by Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.10">Lu 9:10</reference>) as "belonging to the city called Bethsaida." This must not be confounded with the town so called on the western side of the lake (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">Mt 11:21</reference>). This town lay on its northeastern side, near where the Jordan empties itself into it: in Gaulonitis, out of the dominions of Herod Antipas, and within the dominions of Philip the Tetrarch (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.1">Lu 3:1</reference>), who raised it from a village to a city, and called it Julias, in honor of Julia, the daughter of Augustus [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.2,1]. <div eID="gen26934" type="x-p"/>
entries.608e4cc7abdbe821b27e1616050b91f58f7b6400: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13982"/><div sID="gen26935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13982"/><hi type="bold">33. And the people--</hi>the multitudes.<div eID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw them departing, and many knew him--</hi>The true reading would seem to be: "And many saw them departing, and knew or recognized [them]."<div eID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ran afoot--</hi>Here, perhaps, it should be rendered "by land"--running round by the head of the lake, and taking one of the fords of the river, so as to meet Jesus, who was crossing with the Twelve by ship.<div eID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thither out of all cities, and outwent them--</hi>got before them.<div eID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and came together unto him--</hi>How exceedingly graphic is this! every touch of it betokening the presence of an eye-witness. John (<reference osisRef="John.6.3">Joh 6:3</reference>) says, that "Jesus went up into a mountain"--somewhere in that hilly range, the green tableland which skirts the eastern side of the lake. <div eID="gen26939" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcb252ef40ca8761d9f6ad0607c6208593f5bcb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13983"/><div sID="gen26940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13983"/><hi type="bold">34. And Jesus, when he came out of the ship--</hi>having gone on shore.<div eID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saw much people--</hi>a great multitude.<div eID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd--</hi>At the sight of the multitudes who had followed Him by land and even got before Him, He was so moved, as was His wont in such cases, with compassion, because they were like shepherdless sheep, as to forego both privacy and rest that He might minister to them. Here we have an important piece of information from the Fourth Evangelist (<reference osisRef="John.6.4">Joh 6:4</reference>), "And the passover, a feast of the Jews, was nigh"--rather, "Now the passover, the feast of the Jews, was nigh." This accounts for the multitudes that now crowded around Him. They were on their way to keep that festival at Jerusalem. But Jesus did not go up to this festival, as John expressly tells us, (<reference osisRef="John.7.1">Joh 7:1</reference>)--remaining in Galilee, because the ruling Jews sought to kill Him. <div eID="gen26942" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fc4d9eb8078a2ecade537c9d206f9c649bf93ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13984"/><div sID="gen26943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13984"/><hi type="bold">35. And when the day was now far spent--</hi>"began to wear away" or "decline," says Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.12">Lu 9:12</reference>). Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.15">Mt 14:15</reference>) says, "when it was evening"; and yet he mentions a later evening of the same day (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.23">Mr 6:23</reference>). This earlier evening began at three P.M.; the latter began at sunset. <div eID="gen26943" type="x-p"/>
entries.47e1dddecad869fc03a046b3e113b688b5c83684: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13985"/><div sID="gen26944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13985"/><hi type="bold">36. Send them away, that they may go into the country round about, and into the villages, and buy themselves bread: for they have nothing to eat--</hi>John tells us (<reference osisRef="John.6.5">Joh 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.6">6</reference>) that "Jesus said to Philip, Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat? (And this He said to prove him: for He Himself knew what He would do)." The subject may have been introduced by some remark of the disciples; but the precise order and form of what was said by each can hardly be gathered with precision, nor is it of any importance. <div eID="gen26944" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0c3657932bd14b9b8f55883d6841c5bcd85f20b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13986"/><div sID="gen26945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13986"/><hi type="bold">37. He answered and said unto them--</hi>"They need not depart" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.10">Mt 14:10</reference>).<div eID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Give ye them to eat--</hi>doubtless said to prepare them for what was to follow.<div eID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?--</hi>"Philip answered Him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little" (<reference osisRef="John.6.7">Joh 6:7</reference>). <div eID="gen26947" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d3c3776ad2833f4ac4b8add2bbca53a429b3fa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13987"/><div sID="gen26948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13987"/><hi type="bold">38. He saith unto them, How many loaves have ye? go and see. And when they knew, they say, Five, and two fishes--</hi>John is more precise and full: "One of His disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, saith unto Him, There is a lad here which hath five barley loaves and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" (<reference osisRef="John.6.8">Joh 6:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.9">9</reference>). Probably this was the whole stock of provisions then at the command of the disciples--no more than enough for one meal to them--and entrusted for the time to this lad. "He said, Bring them hither to me" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.18">Mt 14:18</reference>). <div eID="gen26948" type="x-p"/>
entries.d92ed5b3a51f069abf67d07290ece94aa42e66ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13988"/><div sID="gen26949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13988"/><hi type="bold">39. And he commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass--</hi>or "green hay"; the rank grass of those bushy wastes. For, as John (<reference osisRef="John.6.10">Joh 6:10</reference>) notes, "there was much grass in the place." <div eID="gen26949" type="x-p"/>
entries.0682549a09e0af5f6f94cf4d78e90875fde8ff9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13989"/><div sID="gen26950" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13989"/><hi type="bold">40. And they sat down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties--</hi>Doubtless this was to show at a glance the number fed, and to enable all to witness in an orderly manner this glorious miracle. <div eID="gen26950" type="x-p"/>
entries.49e29517861f3de3e68846d1d6689b152b693bf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13990"/><div sID="gen26951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13990"/><hi type="bold">41. And when he had taken the five loaves and the two fishes, he looked up to heaven--</hi>Thus would the most distant of them see distinctly what He was doing.<div eID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and blessed--</hi>John (<reference osisRef="John.6.11">Joh 6:11</reference>) says, "And when he had given thanks." The sense is the same. This thanksgiving for the meal, and benediction of it as the food of thousands, was the crisis of the miracle.<div eID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and brake the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before them--</hi>thus virtually holding forth these men as His future ministers.<div eID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> and the two fishes divided he among them all. <div eID="gen26954" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad81edf023f0761fd377457ed0aeabc4d02b5088: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13991"/><div sID="gen26955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13991"/><hi type="bold">42. And they did all eat, and were filled--</hi>All the four Evangelists mention this: and John (<reference osisRef="John.6.11">Joh 6:11</reference>) adds, "and likewise of the fishes, as much as they would"--to show that vast as was the multitude, and scanty the provisions, the meal to each and all of them was a plentiful one. "When they were filled, He said unto His disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost" (<reference osisRef="John.6.12">Joh 6:12</reference>). This was designed to bring out the whole extent of the miracle. <div eID="gen26955" type="x-p"/>
entries.b23322fd8e3a2aa1015128d98a75f3dbb0388343: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13992"/><div sID="gen26956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13992"/><hi type="bold">43. And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments, and of the fishes--</hi>"Therefore (says <reference osisRef="John.6.13">Joh 6:13</reference>), they gathered them together, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten." The article here rendered "baskets" in all the four narratives was part of the luggage taken by Jews on a journey--to carry, it is said, both their provisions and hay to sleep on, that they might not have to depend on Gentiles, and so run the risk of ceremonial pollution. In this we have a striking corroboration of the truth of the four narratives. Internal evidence renders it clear, we think, that the first three Evangelists wrote independently of each other, though the fourth must have seen all the others. But here, each of the first three Evangelists uses the same word to express the apparently insignificant circumstance that the baskets employed to gather up the fragments were of the kind which even the Roman satirist, Juvenal, knew by the name of cophinus, while in both the narratives of the feeding of the Four Thousand the baskets used are expressly said to have been of the kind called spuris. (See <reference osisRef="Mark.8.19">Mr 8:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.20">20</reference>.) <div eID="gen26956" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cfe9c9de74fb370fd6fea7d1bce3ca928d51424: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13993"/><div sID="gen26957" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13993"/><hi type="bold">44. And they that did eat of the loaves were about five thousand men--</hi>"besides women and children" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.21">Mt 14:21</reference>). Of these, however, there would probably not be many; as only the males were obliged to go to the approaching festival.<div eID="gen26957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> Jesus Recrosses to the Western side of the Lake Walking on the Sea (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.45-Mark.6.56">Mr 6:45-56</reference>).<div eID="gen26958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26959" type="x-p"/> One very important particular given by John alone (<reference osisRef="John.6.15">Joh 6:15</reference>) introduces this portion: "When Jesus therefore perceived that they would take Him by force, to make Him a king, He departed again into a mountain Himself alone." <div eID="gen26959" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a687f10b980a8a3f2e4c9df1dd43d1f2cb4400f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13994"/><div sID="gen26960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13994"/><hi type="bold">45. And straightway he constrained his disciples to get into the ship, and to go to the other side before--</hi>Him.<div eID="gen26960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Bethsaida--</hi>Bethsaida of Galilee (<reference osisRef="John.12.21">Joh 12:21</reference>). John (<reference osisRef="John.6.17">Joh 6:17</reference>) says they "went over the sea towards Capernaum"--the wind, probably, occasioning this slight deviation from the direction of Bethsaida.<div eID="gen26961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">while he sent away the people--</hi>"the multitude." His object in this was to put an end to the misdirected excitement in His favor (<reference osisRef="John.6.15">Joh 6:15</reference>), into which the disciples themselves may have been somewhat drawn. The word "constrained" implies reluctance on their part, perhaps from unwillingness to part with their Master and embark at night, leaving Him alone on the mountain. <div eID="gen26962" type="x-p"/>
entries.91ea3db2e21f3cc47ca0c0ae65ed84a085ebec63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13995"/><div sID="gen26963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13995"/><hi type="bold">46. And when he had sent them away, he departed into a mountain to pray--</hi>thus at length getting that privacy and rest which He had vainly sought during the earlier part of the day; opportunity also to pour out His soul in connection with the extraordinary excitement in His favor that evening--which appears to have marked the zenith of His reputation, for it began to decline the very next day; and a place whence He might watch the disciples on the lake, pray for them in their extremity, and observe the right time for coming to them, in a new manifestation of His glory, on the sea. <div eID="gen26963" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dcdab5af36c6b484748e1bb5976a600ee37de13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13996"/><div sID="gen26964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13996"/><hi type="bold">47. And when even was come--</hi>the later evening (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.35">Mr 6:35</reference>). It had come even when the disciples embarked (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.23">Mt 14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.16">Joh 6:16</reference>).<div eID="gen26964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the ship was in the midst of the sea, and he alone on the land--</hi>John says (<reference osisRef="John.6.17">Joh 6:17</reference>), "It was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them." Perhaps they made no great effort to push across at first, having a lingering hope that their Master would yet join them, and so allowed the darkness to come on. "And the sea arose" (adds the beloved disciple, <reference osisRef="John.6.18">Joh 6:18</reference>), "by reason of a great wind that blew." <div eID="gen26965" type="x-p"/>
entries.272919a35520736fd62d1ee2586691b305b3e616: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13997"/><div sID="gen26966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13997"/><hi type="bold">48. And he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them--</hi>putting forth all their strength to buffet the waves and bear on against a head wind, but to little effect. He "saw" this from His mountain top, and through the darkness of the night, for His heart was all with them: yet would He not go to their relief till His own time came.<div eID="gen26966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and about the fourth watch of the night--</hi>The Jews, who used to divide the night into three watches, latterly adopted the Roman division into four watches, as here. So that, at the rate of three hours to each, the fourth watch, reckoning from six P.M., would be three o'clock in the morning. "So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs" (<reference osisRef="John.6.19">Joh 6:19</reference>)--rather more than halfway across. The lake is about seven miles broad at its widest part. So that in eight or nine hours they had only made some three and a half miles. By this time, therefore, they must have been in a state of exhaustion and despondency bordering on despair; and now at length, having tried them long enough.<div eID="gen26967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he cometh unto them, walking upon the sea--</hi>"and draweth nigh unto the ship" (<reference osisRef="John.6.19">Joh 6:19</reference>).<div eID="gen26968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and would have passed by them--</hi>but only in the sense of <reference osisRef="Luke.24.28">Lu 24:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Ge 32:26</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.3">Ge 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.42.7">42:7</reference>. <div eID="gen26969" type="x-p"/>
entries.a14f2e135146f63b92fdf6d7bbb51b36abed5fd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13998"/><div sID="gen26970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13998"/><hi type="bold">49. But when they saw him walking upon the sea, they supposed it had been a spirit, and cried out--</hi>"for fear" (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.26">Mt 14:26</reference>). He would appear to them at first like a dark moving speck upon the waters; then as a human figure; but in the dark tempestuous sky, and not dreaming that it could be their Lord, they take it for a spirit. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.24.37">Lu 24:37</reference>. <div eID="gen26970" type="x-p"/>
entries.560a749a0ff6bacd7b4d4dce87894a74bf1e9130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13999"/><div sID="gen26971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13999"/><hi type="bold">50. For they all saw him, and were troubled. And immediately he talked with them, and saith unto them, Be of good cheer: It is I; be not afraid--</hi>There is something in these two little words--given by Matthew, Mark and John (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.27">Mt 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.50">Mr 6:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.20">Joh 6:20</reference>)--"It is I," which from the mouth that spake it and the circumstances in which it was uttered, passes the power of language to express. Here were they in the midst of a raging sea, their little bark the sport of the elements, and with just enough of light to descry an object on the waters which only aggravated their fears. But Jesus deems it enough to dispel all apprehension to let them know that He was there. From other lips that "I am" would have merely meant that the person speaking was such a one and not another person. That, surely, would have done little to calm the fears of men expecting every minute, it may be, to go to the bottom. But spoken by One who at that moment was "treading upon the waves of the sea," and was about to hush the raging elements with His word, what was it but the Voice which cried of old in the ears of Israel, even from the days of Moses, "I AM"; "I, EVEN I, AM He!" Compare <reference osisRef="John.18.5">Joh 18:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.18.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.58">8:58</reference>. Now, that Word is "made flesh, and dwells among us," uttering itself from beside us in dear familiar tones--"It is the Voice of my Beloved!" How far was this apprehended by these frightened disciples? There was one, we know, in the boat who outstripped all the rest in susceptibility to such sublime appeals. It was not the deep-toned writer of the Fourth Gospel, who, though he lived to soar beyond all the apostles, was as yet too young for prominence, and all unripe. It was Simon Barjonas. Here follows a very remarkable and instructive episode, recorded by Matthew alone:<div eID="gen26971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> Peter Ventures to Walk upon the Sea (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.28-Matt.14.32">Mt 14:28-32</reference>).<div eID="gen26972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.28">Mt 14:28</reference>:<div eID="gen26973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And Peter answered Him, and said, Lord, If it be Thou, bid me come unto Thee on the water--</hi>not "let me," but "give me the word of command"--"command," or "order me to come unto Thee upon the waters."<div eID="gen26974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.29">Mt 14:29</reference>:<div eID="gen26975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And He said, Come--</hi>Sublime word, issuing from One conscious of power over the raging element, to bid it serve both Himself and whomsoever else He pleased!<div eID="gen26976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked upon the water--</hi>"waters."<div eID="gen26977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to come to Jesus--</hi>"It was a bold spirit," says Bishop Hall, "that could wish it; more bold that could act it--not fearing either the softness or the roughness of that uncouth passage."<div eID="gen26978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.30">Mt 14:30</reference>:<div eID="gen26979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid: and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me--</hi>The wind was as boisterous before, but Peter "saw" it not, seeing only the power of Christ, in the lively exercise of faith. Now he "sees" the fury of the elements, and immediately the power of Christ to bear him up fades before his view, and this makes him "afraid"--as how could he be otherwise, without any felt power to keep him up? He then "begins to sink"; and finally, conscious that his experiment had failed, he casts himself, in a sort of desperate confidence, upon his "Lord" for deliverance!<div eID="gen26980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.31">Mt 14:31</reference>:<div eID="gen26981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And immediately Jesus stretched forth His hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?--</hi>This rebuke was not administered while Peter was sinking, nor till Christ had him by the hand: first reinvigorating his faith, and then with it enabling him again to walk upon the crested wave. Useless else had been this loving reproof, which owns the faith that had ventured on the deep upon the bare word of Christ, but asks why that distrust which so quickly marred it.<div eID="gen26982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.14.32">Mt 14:32</reference>:<div eID="gen26983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And when they--</hi>Jesus and Peter.<div eID="gen26984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26985" type="x-p"/> were come into the ship, the wind ceased. <div eID="gen26985" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff90a896df7c58c69dd093ed3250d18cc63d1090: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14000"/><div sID="gen26986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14000"/><hi type="bold">51. And he went up unto them into the ship--</hi>John (<reference osisRef="John.6.21">Joh 6:21</reference>) says, "Then they willingly received him into the ship"--or rather, "Then were they willing to receive Him" (with reference to their previous terror); but implying also a glad welcome, their first fears now converted into wonder and delight. "And immediately," adds the beloved disciple, "they were at the land whither they went," or "were bound." This additional miracle, for as such it is manifestly related, is recorded by the fourth Evangelist alone. As the storm was suddenly calmed, so the little bark--propelled by the secret power of the Lord of nature now sailing in it--glided through the now unruffled waters, and, while they were wrapt in wonder at what had happened, not heeding their rapid motion, was found at port, to their still further surprise.<div eID="gen26986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> "Then are they glad, because at rest<div eID="gen26987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> And quiet now they be;<div eID="gen26988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> So to the haven He them brings<div eID="gen26989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> Which they desired to see."<div eID="gen26990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.33">Mt 14:33</reference>) says, "Then they that were in the ship came [that is, ere they got to land] and worshipped him, saying, Of a truth Thou art the Son of God." But our Evangelist is wonderfully striking.<div eID="gen26991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the wind ceased and they were sore amazed in themselves beyond measure, and wondered--</hi>The Evangelist seems hardly to find language strong enough to express their astonishment. <div eID="gen26992" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6ffbce4a936d2ff7950ae414e91ecfe6a9b3f87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14001"/><div sID="gen26993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14001"/><hi type="bold">52. For they considered not the miracle of the loaves; for their heart was hardened--</hi>What a singular statement! The meaning seems to be that if they had but "considered [reflected upon] the miracle of the loaves," wrought but a few hours before, they would have wondered at nothing which He might do within the whole circle of power and grace.<div eID="gen26993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> Incidents on Landing (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.53-Mark.6.56">Mr 6:53-56</reference>).<div eID="gen26994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26995" type="x-p"/> The details here are given with a rich vividness quite peculiar to this charming Gospel. <div eID="gen26995" type="x-p"/>
entries.dabd7cd2cfcb8cc1db64917aa7944cf22faaa453: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14002"/><div sID="gen26996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14002"/><hi type="bold">53. And when they had passed over, they came into the land of Gennesaret--</hi>from which the lake sometimes takes its name, stretching along its western shore. Capernaum was their landing-place (<reference osisRef="John.6.24">Joh 6:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen26996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and drew to the shore--</hi>a nautical phrase, nowhere else used in the New Testament. <div eID="gen26997" type="x-p"/>
entries.849ea0cf229a7472ead21b4b98c1c8e68793d967: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14003"/><div sID="gen26998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14003"/><hi type="bold">54. And when they were come out of the ship, straightway they knew him--</hi>"immediately they recognized Him"; that is, the people did. <div eID="gen26998" type="x-p"/>
entries.67a730e5fc9d33f56b751215d697e7700c705be7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14004"/><div sID="gen26999" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14004"/><hi type="bold">55. and began to carry about in beds those that were sick, where they heard he was--</hi>At this period of our Lord's ministry the popular enthusiasm in His favor was at its height. <div eID="gen26999" type="x-p"/>
entries.1312490b1b3dc4be9e4e994409e35e041c85005e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14005"/><div sID="gen27000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14005"/><hi type="bold">56. and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment--</hi>having heard, no doubt, of what the woman with the issue of blood experienced on doing so (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.25-Mark.5.29">Mr 5:25-29</reference>), and perhaps of other unrecorded cases of the same nature.<div eID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and as many as touched him--</hi>or "it"--the border of His garment.<div eID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were made whole--</hi>All this they continued to do and to experience while our Lord was in that region. The time corresponds to that mentioned (<reference osisRef="John.7.1">Joh 7:1</reference>), when He "walked in Galilee," instead of appearing in Jerusalem at the passover, "because the Jews," that is, the rulers, "sought to kill Him"--while the people sought to enthrone Him! <chapter eID="Mark.6"/>

entries.75f0728af05ea8d9c34326cf3ad4d4e0d2bb0c5c: <div eID="gen39320" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39321" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39322" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39322" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39321" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39323" type="x-p"/> Our Lord's countrymen are astonished at his wisdom and mighty works, and are offended at him, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.1-Mar.6.4">Mar 6:1-4</reference>. He works few miracles there, because of their unbelief, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.5">Mar 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.6">Mar 6:6</reference>. He sends forth his disciples by two and two to preach, etc., <reference osisRef="Mar.6.7-Mar.6.11">Mar 6:7-11</reference>. They depart, preach, and work miracles, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.12">Mar 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.13">Mar 6:13</reference>. Different opinions of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.14-Mar.6.16">Mar 6:14-16</reference>. Account of the beheading of John Baptist, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.17-Mar.6.29">Mar 6:17-29</reference>. The disciples return, and give an account of their mission, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.30">Mar 6:30</reference>. He departs with them to a place of privacy, but the people follow him, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.31-Mar.6.33">Mar 6:31-33</reference>. He has compassion on them, and miraculously feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fishes, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.34-Mar.6.44">Mar 6:34-44</reference>. He sends the disciples by sea to Bethsaida, and himself goes into a mountain to pray, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.46">Mar 6:46</reference>. The disciples meet with a storm, and he comes to them walking upon the water, and appeases the winds and the sea, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.47-Mar.6.52">Mar 6:47-52</reference>. They come into the land of Gennesaret, and he works many miracles, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.53-Mar.6.56">Mar 6:53-56</reference>. <div eID="gen39323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39324" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39325" type="x-p"/> And he went out from thence - That is, from Capernaum. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.13.54">Mat 13:54</reference> (note).
entries.4c2fc0c2c941da6168780f7ca46fb6c836de6043: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39326" type="x-p"/> Were astonished - επι τῃ διδαχῃ αυτου, at his doctrine, or teaching. This is added by the Codex Bezae and eight others, later Syriac, Armenian, Vulgate, and all the Itala.
entries.d5647f7a17791ba49a9934cec3ff8f2f8b7ecc2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39327" type="x-p"/> Is not this the carpenter - Among the ancient Jews, every father was bound to do four things for his son. <div eID="gen39327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39328" type="x-p"/> 1. To circumcise him. <div eID="gen39328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39329" type="x-p"/> 2. To redeem him. <div eID="gen39329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39330" type="x-p"/> 3. To teach him the law. <div eID="gen39330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39331" type="x-p"/> 4. To teach him a trade. <div eID="gen39331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39332" type="x-p"/> And this was founded on the following just maxim: "He who teaches not his son to do some work, is as if he taught him robbery!" It is therefore likely that Joseph brought up our Lord to his own trade. <div eID="gen39332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39333" type="x-p"/> Joses - Several good MSS. read Ιωσητος, Joset, and one, with several versions, reads Joseph.
entries.f28826b84abd538fd6e48d10d5d1814315528ac8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39334" type="x-p"/> See this curious subject explained, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.55-Mat.13.58">Mat 13:55-58</reference> (note).
entries.a655357354a7e32a44a21fafd347494d350fc35c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39335" type="x-p"/> By two and two - That they might encourage and support each other; and to show that union among the ministers of the Gospel is essential to the promotion of the cause of truth. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.10.1">Luk 10:1</reference> (note).
entries.1457d73453e38133f3fc099023b45ab59c057140: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39336" type="x-p"/> A staff only - It is likely he desired them to take only one with every two, merely for the purpose of carrying any part of their clothes on, when they should be obliged to strip them off by reason of the heat; for walking staves, or things of this kind, were forbidden, see <reference osisRef="Mat.10.10">Mat 10:10</reference>. But, probably, no more is designed than simply to state that they must not wait to make any provision for the journey, but go off just as they were, leaving the provision necessary in the present case to the care of Divine Providence. St. James is represented in ancient paintings, as carrying a gourd bottle on a Staff across his shoulder.
entries.6d79d3aa8a9b3ef3e37e70e0a6ec275e905477ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39337" type="x-p"/> Shod with sandals - The sandal seems to have been similar to the Roman solea, which covered only the sole of the foot, and was fastened about the foot and ankle with straps. The sandal was originally a part of the woman's dress; ancient authors represent them as worn only by women. In <reference osisRef="Mat.10.10">Mat 10:10</reference>, the disciples are commanded to take no shoes, ὑποδηματα, which word is nearly of the same import with σανδαλια, sandals; but, as our Lord intimates to them that they should be free from all useless incumbrances, that they might fulfill his orders with the utmost diligence and despatch, so we may suppose that the sandal was a lighter kind of wear than the shoe: and indeed the word sandal, which is mere Chaldee, סנדל might be properly translated a light shoe; as it is compounded of סין sin, a shoe, (see Targum, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.9">Deu 25:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.25.10">Deu 25:10</reference>), and דל dal, thin, slender, or mean, as being made, not only lighter than the hypodema or shoe, but (probably) also of meaner materials. See many excellent observations on this subject in Martinius's Etymolog. Lexicon, under the word Sandalium.
entries.a30635eed6d2b54963e62856433479915023396d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39338" type="x-p"/> And whosoever shall not receive you - Ὁς αν τοπος μη δεξηται, whatsoever Place will not receive you: this is the reading of BL, four others, and the later Syriac in the margin. <div eID="gen39338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39339" type="x-p"/> Verily, etc. - All this clause is omitted in BCDL, two others, one Arabic, one Persic, Coptic, Armenian, Vulgate, and all the Itala but three. Mill and Beza approve of the omission, and Griesbach leaves it out of the text. It has probably been transferred here from <reference osisRef="Mat.10.15">Mat 10:15</reference>. See this subject, from <reference osisRef="Mar.6.7-Mar.6.11">Mar 6:7-11</reference>, explained at large on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.1-Mat.10.15">Mat 10:1-15</reference> (note).
entries.83a88ff5583cee2a1b2b7125fd346b0de2ab92a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39340" type="x-p"/> Anointed with oil many that were sick - This is only spoken of here, and in <reference osisRef="Jam.5.14">Jam 5:14</reference>. This ceremony was in great use among the Jews; and in certain cases it might be profitable. But in the cases mentioned here, which were merely miraculous, it could avail no more of itself than the imposition of hands. It was used symbolically, as an emblem of that ease, comfort, and joy, which they prayed God to impart to the sick. For various examples of its use among the Jews, see Lightfoot and Wetstein on this place.
entries.c1e263b4358e7a22d24d54ece026eae92cf731da: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39341" type="x-p"/> And king Herod heard? - Την ακοην αοτου, his fame, is added by KM, fifteen others, and in the margin of several. It seems necessary to complete the sense.
entries.225119cee3af50195b9e5d66c1a255d538d0e750: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39342" type="x-p"/> Or, as one of the prophets - η, or, is omitted by ABCEGHKLMS - BHV, and one hundred others, Syriac, all the Arabic, all the Persic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Gothic, Slavonic, Vulgate, two Itala, Origen, Victor, and Theophylact. Bengel, Wetstein, and Griesbach leave it out of the text: the omission of it mends the sense much.
entries.6cf2b7f4b7435e679899e26f9e717c0ec9b5255a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39343" type="x-p"/> Would have killed - Εζητει, Sought to kill him. C and five of the Itala. <div eID="gen39343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39344" type="x-p"/> See the whole of this account, from <reference osisRef="Mar.6.17-Mar.6.29">Mar 6:17-29</reference>, explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.2-Mat.14.12">Mat 14:2-12</reference> (note).
entries.577e0528cb6b465a8d70066fd5b028a2c6cd930e: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39345" type="x-p"/> Lords - Μεγιστασιν, probably governors of particular districts. <div eID="gen39345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39346" type="x-p"/> High captains - Χιλιαρχοις; literally, chiefs or captains over a thousand men, military chiefs. <div eID="gen39346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39347" type="x-p"/> Chief estates - Πρωτοις; probably such as might be called nobles by title only, having no office civil or military; probably magistrates. See Kypke an the place.
entries.0ad8a010c3adc64e0dde7edc6b6ef33a1ada3be1: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen39347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39348" type="x-p"/> Unto the half of my kingdom - A noble price for a dance! This extravagance in favor of female dancers has the fullest scope in the east, even to the present day. M. Anquetil du Perron, in the preliminary discourse to his Zend Avesta, p. 344 and 345, gives a particular account of the dancers at Surat. This account cannot be transcribed in a comment on the Gospel of God, however illustrative it might be of the conduct of Herodias and her daughter Salome: it is too abominable for a place here. He observes, that the rich vie with each other in the presents they make to the dancing girls of money and jewels; and that persons of opulence have even ruined themselves by the presents they made to those victims of debauch. He mentions a remarkable case, which may throw light on this passage: "That the dancer Laal-koner gained such a complete ascendancy over the Mogul Emperor Maaz-eddin, that he made her joint governess of the empire with himself."
entries.a386f1039aafee1c3a088b032a9ac10e90bd903e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39349" type="x-p"/> For their sakes which sat with him - Probably these persons joined in with the request, and were glad of this opportunity to get this light of Israel extinguished; he being a public reprover of all their vices.
entries.2c56baf70d915ea8076b091cd0f2c8d324b9c7a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39350" type="x-p"/> The apostles gathered themselves together - For they went different ways before, by two and two, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.7">Mar 6:7</reference>; and now they return and meet Christ at Capernaum.

entries.4e2e0343f0d8e6ac990cc35ff86cc3859ab2eba6: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen39351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39352" type="x-p"/> The people - Or, οχλοι, the multitudes. entries.a56bb7b25b259a957374f2c2bb70c3e3d35412cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39353" type="x-p"/> Much people, etc. - See this miracle explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.14">Mat 14:14</reference> (note), etc.

entries.192df8ba94d630fb1776658f0bd88b0e2f748880: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen39354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39355" type="x-p"/> And blessed - I think the word God should be inserted here, as in <reference osisRef="Mat.14.19">Mat 14:19</reference>. entries.9571fac469696bfd2e06f4d53282a0f615c77d5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen39356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39357" type="x-p"/> Were about five thousand - ὡσει, about, is omitted by a great majority of the best MSS. and by the principal versions. Verse 7. By two and two. In order that they might support and encourage each other in their work. Amidst the trials and opposition which they would meet with, mutual counsel and aid would greatly lighten their burdens, and alleviate their calamities. Mutual counsel might also contribute to their success, and lead to united plans to advance the kingdom of the Redeemer. Jesus here, as in all the work of religion, consulted at the same time the happiness and usefulness of his disciples. Nor are they ever separated. Whatever contributes to the usefulness of the people, produces also their happiness; or, in other words, the secret of being happy, is to be useful.

entries.bf1f9160439ef375ff5b4cfaf34f34066f1bc137:
Verse 13. Cast out many devils. Mt 4:24.

And anointed with oil, etc. Anointing with oil was in common use among the Jews in cases of sickness. It was supposed to have a mild, soothing, and alleviating effect on the body. In Jas 5:14, the elders of the church, in connexion with prayers, were directed also to anoint the sick with oil. It was also used in wounds. The good Samaritan poured in oil and wine into the wounds of the waylaid Jew, Lk 10:34. Josephus says, that in the last sickness of Herod, his physicians commanded him to be anointed with oil. It need not be supposed, however, that the apostles used oil for mere medical purposes. It was used, probably, like the imposition of hands, or like our Saviour's anointing the eyes of the blind with clay, merely as a sign, in expectation of imparting that aid and comfort from God which was sought, and which was represented by the natural, soothing, and gentle effect of oil.

Verse 20. He did many things. But he did not do the thing which was demanded of him--to break off from his sins. He attempted to make a compromise with his conscience. He still loved his sins, and did other things which he supposed might be accepted, in the place of putting away, as he ought, the wife of his brother--the polluted and adulterous woman with whom he lived. Perhaps he treated John kindly, or spoke well of him, or aided him in his wants; and attempted in this way to silence his rebukes, and destroy his faithfulness. This was probably before John was imprisoned. So sinners often treat ministers kindly, and do much to make them comfortable, and hear them gladly, while they are still unwilling to do the thing which is demanded of them, to repent and believe the gospel. They expect that their kind attentions will be accepted in the place of what God demands--repentance and the forsaking of their sins.

Mark 6:12. And they departed, and preached. Matthew silently passes over what the Apostles did. Mark and Luke relate that they proceeded to execute the commission which they had received; and from their statements it appears more clearly, that the office which Christ at that time bestowed upon them, as I have formerly mentioned, was temporary, and indeed lasted but a few days. They tell us that the Apostles went through the cities and villages: and they unquestionably returned in a short time to their Master, as we shall find to be stated in another passage.
The only matter that requires exposition here is the fact related by Mark, that they anointed with oil many diseased persons Christ having conferred on them the power of healing, it is asked, why did they apply oil? Some learned persons suppose that it was a sort of medicine; and I acknowledge that in these countries the use of oil was very common. But nothing is more unreasonable than to imagine, that the Apostles employed ordinary and natural remedies, which would have the effect of obscuring the miracles of Christ. They were not instructed by our Lord in the art and science of healing, but, on the contrary, were enjoined to perform miracles which would arouse all Judea. I think, therefore, that this anointing was a visible token of spiritual grace, by which the healing that was administered by them was declared to proceed from the secret power of God; for under the Law oil was employed to represent the grace of the Spirit. The absurdity of an attempt to imitate the Apostles, by making the anointing of the sick a perpetual ordinance of the Church, appears from the fact, that Christ bestowed on the Apostles the gift of healing, not as an inheritance which they should hand down to posterity, but as a temporary seal of the doctrine of the Gospel. In our own day, the ignorance of the Papists is exceedingly ridiculous in maintaining that their nasty unction,
The allusion is to extreme unction, (or last anointing,) which is one of the Seven Sacraments recognized by the Church of Rome. — Ed.

entries.68afc9bc868685c489a4a45ee5c688b4ce4ab095: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.6.24" sID="gen99859" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.24">Mark 6:24</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And she went out, and said to her mother</hi> We need not wonder that Herodias attached so much importance to John’s death. <note n="367"> <div sID="gen99861" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De ce qu’ Herodias a estime un grand avantage pour elle de faire mourir Iean</foreign>;” — “that Herodias reckoned it a great advantage to her to put John to death.”<div eID="gen99861" type="x-p"/> </note> The conjecture thrown out by some—that she was actuated by revenge,—is not at all probable. It was rather the dread of being cast off that inflamed and tormented her; as it usually happens that, when adulterers are visited with feelings of uneasiness, they become ashamed of their own lust. But she hoped that this crime would bind Herod more closely to her than ever, if the disgrace of a pretended marriage were washed out by the blood of the prophet. That her power might be more secure for the future, she longed for the death of that man whom she imagined to be her only opponent; and this shows us the wretched anxiety by which a bad conscience is always tormented. John was detained in prison, and the haughty and cruel woman might have issued orders that no man should converse with or approach him; and yet she has no rest, but is oppressed with anxiety and alarm, till the prophet be removed out of the way. This likewise serves to show the power of the word of God, that the voice of the holy man, even when shut up in prison, wounds and tortures in the keenest manner the mind of the king’s wife. <note n="368"> <div sID="gen99862" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ne laisse pas d’espouvanter asprement, et navrer au vif le coeur de ceste femme</foreign>;” — “fails not vehmently to alarm and cut to the quick the heart of the woman.”<div eID="gen99862" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen99860" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99859" osisID="Mark.6.24" type="section"/>
entries.e8851de7c055dd2748b269826e0aacbcb389d97f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.6.26" sID="gen99863" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi><hi type="italic"> And the king being sorry.</hi> His heart, as we have said, was no longer influenced by religious sentiments; but, foreseeing the detestation that will be excited by such a crime, he dreads both the loss of character and positive harm, and consequently repents of his levity. And yet he has not the courage to give a refusal to a dancing girl, lest he should incur the reproach of unsteadiness; as if it were more dishonorable to retract a rash and foolish promise than to persist in a heinous crime. With the wonted vanity of kings, he does not choose that what he has once uttered shall be recalled, and orders that the prophet shall be instantly slain. We infer that Herod was at that time supping in the castle of Macherus, where, Josephus tells us, John was imprisoned, (Ant. 18. 5:2.)<div eID="gen99864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99865" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">On account of the oath, and of those who sat at table with him.</hi> It deserves our attention that the Evangelists state this to be the reason of his grief; and hence we infer that, though he had sworn a hundred times, yet if there had been no witness, he would not have held by his oath. No inward feelings of religion constrained Herod to do this, but the mere love of power drove him headlong; for he reckoned that he would sink in the estimation of those who were present, if he did not fulfill his engagement. Thus it frequently happens that ungodly men fail to perform their duty, because they do not look to God, but are only intent on this object, that they may not incur the reproaches of men. <note n="369"> <div sID="gen99866" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et ne se soucient seulement que d’eviter le blasme et la moquerie des hommes</foreign>;”— “and are only anxious to avoid the censure and ridicule of men.”<div eID="gen99866" type="x-p"/> </note> But though Herod had kept before his eyes the sacredness of an oath alone, and not the dread of the opinion of men, he committed a more heinous offense in fulfilling a foolish promise than if he had violated his oath. First, he was deeply in fault for such haste in swearing; for the design of an oath is to confirm a promise in a doubtful matter. Next, when it appeared that he could not be relieved from his engagement without involving himself in an aggravated crime, he had no right to implicate the sacred name of God in such wickedness; for what could be more at variance with the nature of God than to lend his countenance to a shocking murder? If a private loss is at stake, let him who has made a rash oath suffer the punishment of his folly; but, when a man has taken the name of God in vain, let him beware of doubling his guilt by employing this as a pretense for committing some enormous crime. Hence it follows, that monastic vows, which are attended by open impiety, do not bind the conscience any more than the enchantments of magicians; for it is not the will of God that his sacred name shall give support to what is sinful. But this passage teaches us, that we ought to beware of making promises without consideration; and next, that lightness must not be followed by obstinacy.<div eID="gen99865" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99863" osisID="Mark.6.26" type="section"/>
entries.5f79b47c274af3c2928a7ca820d7ed858b16a3bd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.6.28" sID="gen99867" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28. </hi><hi type="italic">And gave it to the girl.</hi> It was an additional aggravation of this detestable crime, that the head of the holy man was made, after his death, a matter of sport. But in this way the Lord sometimes gives up his people to the pride of wicked men, till he at length makes it evident that their blood is <hi type="italic">precious in his sight </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.116.15">Psalm 116:15</reference>.) <hi type="italic">Herodias</hi> is delighted with the thought of having gained her wicked purpose, and cruelly triumphs over her reprover; but when afterwards, stripped of her wealth, and not only deprived of the title of queen, but driven from her native country, and destitute of all means of support, she dragged out a wretched life in poverty and banishment, she presented a spectacle gratifying to angels and to all good people. When we perceive that the guests are compelled to pollute their eyes by beholding this detestable exhibition, let us learn from it, that those who sit at the tables of kings are often involved in many crimes; for, granting that the table is not stained by murder, every thing partakes so largely of all sorts of wickedness, that they who approach to it must be at least given up to debauchery.<div eID="gen99868" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.6.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99867" osisID="Mark.6.28" type="section"/>

29. His disciples came. One thing only remained to complete the woman’s cruelty. It was, to leave the corpse of the holy man unburied; for there is reason to believe that, when his disciples performed this duty, the attendants of the tyrant had thrown out the corpse. Though the honor of burial is of no importance to the dead, yet it is the will of the Lord that we should observe this ceremony as a token of the last resurrection; and therefore God was pleased with the carefulness which was manifested by the disciples, when they came to commit to the tomb the body of their master. Moreover, it was an attestation of their piety; for in this way they declared that the doctrine of their master continued to have a firm hold of their hearts after his death. This confession was therefore worthy of praise, more especially as it was not without danger; for they could not do honor to a man who had been put to death by the executioner without exciting against themselves the rage of the tyrant.
